chapters.summary: Traditional aristocracy derives its legitimacy from spiritual rather than material factors, creating a fundamental distinction between patricians and plebeians.

chapters.title: Spiritual Virility
chapters.summary: Traditional spirituality emphasized direct action and mastery rather than devotional submission, representing a fundamentally masculine approach to transcendence.

chapters.title: The Two Paths in the Afterlife
chapters.summary: Traditional teaching distinguishes between mere survival and true immortality, with most humans dissolving after death while heroes achieve transcendent continuity.

chapters.title: Life and Death of Civilizations
chapters.summary: Civilizations decline when their spiritual center weakens, not due to external material factors, but through loss of connection to transcendent principles.

chapters.title: Initiation and Consecration
chapters.summary: When natural divinity no longer incarnates directly, special ritual actions become necessary to establish connection between human individuals and transcendent functions.

chapters.title: On the Hierarchical Relationship Between Royalty and Priesthood
chapters.summary: When spiritual and temporal powers separate, kingship maintains primacy over priesthood as the active principle over the passive matrix.

chapters.title: Universality and Centralism
chapters.summary: True imperial unity operates through spiritual attraction and inner adhesion rather than material force and administrative centralization.

chapters.title: The Soul of Chivalry
chapters.summary: Medieval knighthood represented a synthesis of warrior action and spiritual realization, creating a supernational aristocracy dedicated to transcendent principles.

chapters.title: The Doctrine of the Castes
chapters.summary: The traditional caste system reflects natural spiritual hierarchies and provides organic framework for human development according to innate capacities.

chapters.title: Professional Associations and the Arts; Slavery
chapters.summary: Traditional arts and crafts possessed sacred dimension and initiatory potential, while slavery institutionalized the spiritual reality of those bound to material existence.

chapters.title: Bipartition of the Traditional Spirit; Asceticism
chapters.summary: Traditional spirituality manifests through two complementary paths - contemplative detachment and heroic action - both leading beyond human limitations.

chapters.title: The Greater and the Lesser Holy War
chapters.summary: Warfare can serve as means for spiritual realization when external combat becomes the method for conquering inner enemies and achieving transcendence.

chapters.title: Games and Victory
chapters.summary: Traditional games and athletic competitions served ritual functions, connecting human achievement with cosmic forces and spiritual realization.

chapters.title: Space, Time, the Earth
chapters.summary: Traditional man experienced qualitative rather than quantitative dimensions, with space and time serving as living matrices of spiritual meaning.

chapters.title: Man and Woman
chapters.summary: Traditional civilizations recognized fundamental spiritual differences between sexes, with distinct but complementary paths toward transcendence.

chapters.title: The Decline of Superior Races
chapters.summary: Modern demographic trends reflect spiritual degeneration, with quantitative population growth masking qualitative decline of truly human elements.

chapters.title: The Doctrine of the Four Ages
chapters.summary: Traditional humanity universally taught that history represents decline from originally divine states through four successive ages of increasing materialization and spiritual darkness.

chapters.title: The Golden Age
chapters.summary: The primordial era represented pure manifestation of traditional principles when divine beings lived directly among humanity in a state of immortal perfection.

chapters.title: The Pole and the Hyperborean Region
chapters.summary: The primordial age can be associated with specific geographical and symbolic representations centered on polar symbolism, which represents spiritual stability and the supreme center of the world.

chapters.title: The Northern-Atlantic Cycle
chapters.summary: Two great migratory waves can be distinguished: first from north to south, second from west to east, establishing a new Atlantic center that reproduced the polar function.

chapters.title: North and South
chapters.summary: The Atlantic cycle shows typical alteration and differentiation from Hyperborean polar symbolism, revealing fundamental opposition between Northern and Southern spiritual orientations.

chapters.title: The Civilization of the Mother
chapters.summary: This civilization type represents transposition of woman as principle of generation into metaphysical realm, with goddess expressing supreme reality while all beings appear as conditioned and subordinated.

chapters.title: The Cycles of Decadence and the Heroic Cycle
chapters.summary: Biblical tradition mentions race of "heroes of old" born from union of sons of heaven and daughters of men, representing miscegenation that caused primordial spirituality to give way to age of the Mother.

chapters.title: Tradition and Antitradition
chapters.summary: The American and Eastern Mediterranean cycles show different developments of civilizational forces, with Western world being crucial for understanding processes leading to modern world.

chapters.title: The Heroic-Uranian Western Cycle
chapters.summary: Hellenic civilization shows two aspects: one connected to traditional sacred meanings, another anticipating humanistic rationalistic cycle that moderns regard as origin of their civilization.

chapters.title: Syncope of the Western Tradition
chapters.summary: The advent of Christianity marked unprecedented decline, representing subversive character despite presence of some traditional elements within later Catholicism.

chapters.title: The Revival of the Empire and the Ghibelline Middle Ages
chapters.summary: Christianity conquered Western world only superficially as faith while real life continued following opposite tradition of action and Northern-Aryan ethos.

chapters.title: Decline of the Medieval World and the Birth of Nations
chapters.summary: The Holy Roman Empire's decadence was determined by causes from above and below, with gradual secularization and materialization of the political idea.

chapters.title: Unrealism and Individualism
chapters.summary: Modern civilization centers everything in human/temporal world, replacing experience of superworld with ephemeral ghosts and by-products of merely human nature.

chapters.title: The Regression of the Castes
chapters.summary: Progressive shift of power and civilization type has occurred from one caste to next since prehistoric times, representing objective law of decadence process.

chapters.title: Nationalism and Collectivism
chapters.summary: Modern civilization is essentially under the aegis of collectivism, with the collective being to the universal what "matter" is to "form."

chapters.title: The End of the Cycle
chapters.summary: The Bolshevik revolution displayed traits worth examining, showing characteristics of terminal point of every cycle where forces of darkness work openly.
